semantic_correction.stem: A client on the kidney-transplant waiting list says, 'I am anxious because I do not know when an organ offer will come.' Which nursing response is best?

options.A: Acknowledge the uncertainty, review reliable waitlist information, encourage questions about personal status with the transplant team, and offer peer or support resources if desired.
options.B: Reassure the client that an organ offer should occur within a predictable period because time already spent waiting is the main factor that determines kidney availability.
options.C: Limit discussion of the waiting process to required appointments and avoid additional information, because reviewing allocation factors generally increases uncertainty and anxiety.
options.D: Explain that placement on the national waitlist means a suitable kidney will eventually be offered, so additional coping or support resources are usually unnecessary.

semantic_correction.rationale: A is correct. Current HRSA/OPTN patient guidance states that transplant waiting times vary widely and depend on multiple factors, including blood type, tissue type, candidate and organ characteristics, medical urgency, time on the waiting list, donor availability, geography, and the types of organ offers a transplant hospital will accept. Kidney-specific HRSA guidance likewise explains that deceased-donor kidney offers are produced through a matching system that considers medical and allocation factors rather than elapsed waiting time alone. HRSA directs candidates to their transplant hospital for questions about their own waiting-list status and medical care, while OPTN patient services can provide general transplant and policy information. HRSA's kidney-transplant FAQ also identifies doctors, patient support groups, and other people who have been treated for kidney disease as sources of information and support and emphasizes continued regular contact with the transplant program while waiting. Therefore the nurse should acknowledge the uncertainty, provide accurate general information, direct personal status questions to the transplant team, and offer optional support resources without promising when an organ offer will occur. B is incorrect because waiting time is only one of several allocation factors and cannot establish a predictable offer date. C is incorrect because withholding reliable information and support is not justified. D is incorrect because listing does not guarantee that a suitable kidney will eventually be offered and does not eliminate psychosocial support needs.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Support kidney-transplant waitlist anxiety with therapeutic acknowledgment, accurate information about variable allocation factors, appropriate transplant-team communication, and optional peer or support resources without giving false predictions or guarantees about organ availability.

audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item tests therapeutic support of transplant-waitlist uncertainty with one clearly best response, balanced alternatives, current federal transplant guidance, and no answer-length cue.

option_audit.A: Correct. It acknowledges uncertainty, provides reliable general information, directs personal status questions appropriately, and offers optional support without promising an organ-offer date.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. Waiting time is only one of multiple allocation and matching factors, so a predictable offer date cannot be inferred from time already spent waiting.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. Reliable transplant information and appropriate discussion can support informed coping; withholding information is not an evidence-based response to uncertainty.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. Placement on the waitlist does not guarantee a suitable kidney offer and does not eliminate the client's need for coping or support resources.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A uniquely combines therapeutic acknowledgment, accurate information, appropriate transplant-team routing, and optional support; B and D create false certainty, while C withholds useful information and support.
cueing_check: All four options are parallel nursing responses of comparable length and specificity; the prior uniquely-long correct response was removed and no absolute-word or formatting cue identifies the key.
